meta_title: Regression Model in R Programming + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Fit and read a linear regression in R with lm(), summary(), coefficients, R-squared, residuals and predict(). Test yourself with a free 8-question quiz.

quiz.title: R Regression Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on fitting and interpreting linear models in R — lm(), coefficients, summary(), R-squared, predict() and residuals. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Linear regression with lm() in R

questions.q: Which call fits a simple linear regression of y on x in a data frame df?
questions.explanation: The formula interface is response ~ predictor, with the data frame passed via the data argument: lm(y ~ x, data = df).

questions.q: In the formula y ~ x, what does the tilde (~) separate?
questions.explanation: In an R formula the response variable sits on the left of ~ and the predictor(s) on the right. So y ~ x models y as a function of x.

questions.q: You run summary(model). Which value tells you the proportion of variance in y explained by the model?
questions.explanation: Multiple R-squared is the fraction of variance in the response explained by the predictors, ranging from 0 to 1.

questions.q: In the coefficients table, the Estimate for x is 2.5. How do you read it?
options: A one-unit rise in x is linked to a 2.5-unit change in y, holding else equal
questions.explanation: A slope coefficient is the expected change in the response for a one-unit increase in that predictor, with other predictors held constant.

questions.q: Which extractor returns just the fitted intercept and slope from a model object?
questions.explanation: coef(model) (or coefficients(model)) returns the named vector of estimated coefficients, including the intercept.

questions.q: To predict y for new x values stored in a data frame newdf, which call is correct?
questions.explanation: predict() takes the fitted model and a newdata data frame whose columns match the predictor names used in the formula.

questions.q: What does a residual represent in a fitted regression?
options: The observed y minus the fitted y
questions.explanation: A residual is observed minus fitted (y - y-hat). residuals(model) returns them; small, patternless residuals suggest a good fit.

questions.q: How do you add a second predictor z to the model y ~ x?
options: lm(y ~ x : z only, data = df)
questions.explanation: Add predictors with + on the right of the formula: y ~ x + z fits a multiple regression on both x and z.

faq.q: What does the lm() function do in R?
faq.a: lm() fits a linear model by least squares. You give it a formula like y ~ x and a data frame, and it returns a model object holding the coefficients, fitted values and residuals that the other functions read.

faq.q: How do I read the output of summary(model)?
faq.a: Look at the coefficients table for each estimate, its standard error and p-value, then check Multiple R-squared for how much variance is explained and the F-statistic for whether the model as a whole is significant.

faq.q: What is the difference between R-squared and adjusted R-squared?
faq.a: R-squared always rises when you add predictors, even useless ones. Adjusted R-squared penalises extra terms, so it is the fairer number to compare models with different numbers of predictors.

faq.q: How do I make predictions from a fitted model?
faq.a: Use predict(model, newdata = newdf), where newdf is a data frame whose columns have the same names as the predictors in your formula. Without newdata, predict() just returns the fitted values for the training data.
